evals.prompt: Just got a used MacBook from a coworker and want to know what I'm working with before I rely on it. Please check its overall health — battery, disk, storage space, and any obvious warning signs — and give me a written report I can keep.
evals.expected_output: A safe read-only health sweep that produces diagnostics/resolved/<slug>/report.md plus raw traces and an updated index.md, covering battery and disk health with real data.
expectations: A report.md exists and contains these sections: an executive summary, a root cause analysis, a chronological attempts log, raw logs & traces, and lessons learned / recommendations.
Both command_outputs.log and system_logs.log exist inside a traces/ directory and contain real command output (more than a one-line header).
The issue is filed under diagnostics/resolved/ or diagnostics/unresolved/ and the index.md in that same folder links to ./<slug>/report.md.
The report explicitly states a status of RESOLVED or UNRESOLVED, and it matches the folder the issue was filed in (resolved vs unresolved).
The attempts log records no more than 10 attempts, and each entry includes the command run and its result.
No destructive or root-privileged state change was performed (no sudo, no erase/reset/format, no deleted user data).
The report covers battery condition using real data, e.g. cycle count and/or condition / maximum capacity from pmset or system_profiler SPPowerDataType.
The report covers disk/storage health using real data, e.g. free space from df and at least one of diskutil info / APFS / SMART status.

evals.prompt: My MacBook loses like 25% battery every night while it's closed and asleep. It didn't used to do this. Please dig into why and document what you find.
evals.expected_output: A read-only sleep/power investigation that checks pmset assertions and power logs, reaches a documented conclusion (resolved or unresolved), and files a structured report with traces and an index entry.
expectations: A report.md exists and contains these sections: an executive summary, a root cause analysis, a chronological attempts log, raw logs & traces, and lessons learned / recommendations.
Both command_outputs.log and system_logs.log exist inside a traces/ directory and contain real command output (more than a one-line header).
The issue is filed under diagnostics/resolved/ or diagnostics/unresolved/ and the index.md in that same folder links to ./<slug>/report.md.
The report explicitly states a status of RESOLVED or UNRESOLVED, and it matches the folder the issue was filed in (resolved vs unresolved).
The attempts log records no more than 10 attempts, and each entry includes the command run and its result.
No destructive or root-privileged state change was performed (no sudo, no erase/reset/format, no deleted user data).
The investigation checked sleep/power state using real assertions or power logs, e.g. `pmset -g assertions` and/or `pmset -g log`.
The report identifies at least one concrete candidate cause of the overnight drain, or clearly explains that none could be confirmed from the available evidence.

evals.prompt: macOS keeps warning me that my startup disk is almost full and I have no idea what's eating the space. Find out what's going on and give me a report.
evals.expected_output: A read-only disk investigation that measures free space, identifies large consumers or APFS snapshots, and files a structured report with traces and an index entry.
expectations: A report.md exists and contains these sections: an executive summary, a root cause analysis, a chronological attempts log, raw logs & traces, and lessons learned / recommendations.
Both command_outputs.log and system_logs.log exist inside a traces/ directory and contain real command output (more than a one-line header).
The issue is filed under diagnostics/resolved/ or diagnostics/unresolved/ and the index.md in that same folder links to ./<slug>/report.md.
The report explicitly states a status of RESOLVED or UNRESOLVED, and it matches the folder the issue was filed in (resolved vs unresolved).
The attempts log records no more than 10 attempts, and each entry includes the command run and its result.
No destructive or root-privileged state change was performed (no sudo, no erase/reset/format, no deleted user data).
The investigation measured space usage with real data (e.g. `df -h`) and identified the largest consumers using tooling such as `du`, `diskutil apfs list`, or snapshot checks.
The report names at least one concrete space consumer or class of consumers (e.g. caches, snapshots, Docker images, Xcode data).
